meta: Now AI knows it's wrong, but which way should it fix things? Picture yourself blindfolded on a foggy mountain, feeling with your feet for the steepest way down, one small step at a time. That's gradient descent.

muc.title: Which way to turn?
muc.text: Last time: AI measures how wrong it is with a number called the loss. Now the machine needs to know: which way should it turn the knobs to make that number go down?

muc.title: Blindfolded on a mountain
muc.text: Picture yourself blindfolded on a foggy mountainside. You want to get down to the valley, but you can't see anything.

muc.title: Feel with your feet
muc.text: The only way: feel around with your feet to find where it slopes down the most. Then take a small step that way. Feel again, step again.

muc.title: Height is the error
muc.text: For AI, height is the error. Each spot is one way of setting the knobs. Going down means being less wrong. This way of learning is called gradient descent.

muc.title: Millions of small steps
muc.text: The machine repeats feeling and stepping many, many times, sometimes millions. Each step turns all the knobs at once, and the error drops a little more.

muc.title: Long steps or short steps?
muc.text: Step size matters a lot. Steps too long, and you jump right over the valley and bounce up and down. Steps too short, and you walk forever without getting there.

muc.title: Learn like a machine learns
muc.text: You can learn a new skill this way too. Try a task, ask AI to point out your biggest mistake, fix it a bit, then try again. Each round is a small step, but always in the right direction.

muc.title: Which knob caused the mistake?
muc.text: But there are billions of knobs, and the mistake only shows up at the very end. How do you know which knob is to blame? See you in part 4.
